strengths: Timely and important research direction addressing mechanistic interpretability of VideoLLMs for the first time
Thorough and systematic experimental work across multiple models (4 architectures), tasks (5 VideoQA types), and analysis techniques
Well-designed methodology using TVBench to focus on temporal understanding without static bias and appropriately applying Attention Knockout
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations (particularly Figure 1) and logical progression from high-level findings to detailed analysis
Comprehensive validation including scalability analysis (appendix), generalization across models, open-ended QA, and robustness tests
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and promised code release
Practical validation showing identified effective pathways maintain 51.2% accuracy with only 42% of attention edges
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core findings (cross-frame interactions, mid-layer integration, late-layer generation) confirm intuitive, expected patterns rather than revealing surprising mechanisms

Shallow analysis depth documenting where information flows without explaining what computations occur; Logit Lens analysis is superficial, showing only vocabulary terms rather than semantic operations

Significant generalization concerns: effective pathways identified on Action Antonym task but applied universally; layer ranges vary across models (Table E) suggesting model-specific rather than general findings; analysis limited to VideoQA on short synthetic videos
Selection bias from restricting analysis to correct predictions; no quantification of filtered examples; unclear if incorrect predictions have different information flows
Incomplete causal analysis: large performance gaps between random blocking (40.1%) and effective pathways (51.2%) suggest substantial redundancy/alternative pathways, weakening necessity claims
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; no sample size reporting; small accuracy drops (0.3-1.2% in Table 3) lack uncertainty quantification
Overstated effective pathways analysis: marginal accuracy drops could be within noise; random blocking comparison doesn't validate optimality; no exploration of alternative pathway combinations
Limited practical applications: no reported inference speedup from 58% attention reduction; unclear how mechanistic insights improve model design or training

Task-specific limitations: only visual temporal reasoning tested; multiple-choice QA format constrains findings; generalization to other video understanding tasks (captioning, action localization) unclear

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 4 VideoLLM architectures and multiple benchmarks (TVBench, TOMATO, Video-MME, LongVideoBench) with extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses
Addresses an important research gap by investigating internal mechanisms of VideoLLMs for temporal reasoning, filling a gap left by prior work focusing on external model design
Strong empirical validation with compelling effective pathways analysis (Table 3) showing models retain >95% performance with 37-58% attention edges, demonstrating pathway sufficiency
Solid methodological foundation leveraging established interpretability techniques appropriately with proper controls (random blocking baselines, ImageLLM comparisons) and careful causal tracing
Excellent presentation with clear visualizations (Figs. 1-9) and organized progression from cross-frame interactions to video-language integration to answer generation
Exceptional reproducibility with 32-page appendix, implementation details, multiple robustness checks (signal leakage, window size sensitivity, gradual blocking), and promised code release
Findings generalize well across model scales, architectures, and extend to open-ended QA and long-form videos, demonstrating broad applicability
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily applies existing techniques (Attention Knockout from Geva et al. 2023, Logit Lens) to a new domain without introducing new interpretability methods or theoretical frameworks

Findings are largely confirmatory rather than surprising; the progression from early-layer temporal feature extraction to middle-layer integration to late-layer generation aligns with known transformer properties, limiting novelty of insights

Narrow scope restricted to short VideoQA tasks (8 frames, 12×12 token resolution); unclear how findings generalize to higher-resolution videos, longer sequences, or other video understanding tasks (captioning, action localization)

Limited theoretical depth—paper describes where temporal reasoning occurs but provides insufficient insight into why these patterns emerge or whether they are architectural necessities versus training artifacts; missing engagement with transformer circuit literature

Analysis restricted to correct predictions only, biasing findings toward successful reasoning pathways; failure case analysis limited to one task makes incomplete characterization of error mechanisms; unclear if different pathways activate for incorrect predictions

Causality claims need nuance—blocking pathways shows importance but doesn't prove necessity/sufficiency; alternative information routes through residual connections not fully characterized despite Section G.4 efforts

Circular logic in Logit Lens concept extraction—using hand-picked temporal keywords from prompts then detecting those keywords is unsurprising; lacks unsupervised concept discovery or validation that detected concepts are actually leveraged by model

Lacking statistical rigor—many results show trends without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; probability changes (5-15%) in Figures 2-9 not validated as statistically significant

Unclear practical impact—paper suggests future applications (pathway regularization, early-exit strategies) but provides no demonstrations or evidence these insights yield actual performance improvements; actionability for practitioners limited

Effective pathway layer ranges (Table E) empirically determined from single task; generalization across tasks/datasets not validated; design choices (k=9 window size) appear data-optimized rather than principled
